title: Selecting children with vesicoureteral reflux who are most likely to benefit from antibiotic prophylaxis: application of machine learning to RIVUR
contribution: Two optimal classification trees fitted to the CAP and placebo arms of the RIVUR trial give each child's predicted reduction in recurrent UTI risk from antibiotic prophylaxis (AUC 0.82); the abstract claims that treating only children above a 10% reduction reaches the minimal population rUTI with 40% treated, and among 121 held-out children those whose random arm matched the rule had 7.5% vs 19.4% recurrence.
problem_entry: {ML + DA; AP (pediatric urology)} CAP halves recurrent UTI in children with VUR (RIVUR), but long-term outcomes were underpowered and growth and resistance effects are debated, so one-size-fits-all use is doubtful; clinicians' current personalization is experience-based and opaque; question: whose rUTI risk does CAP reduce most (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: One OCT per trial arm predicts rUTI probability; the difference is each child's CAP benefit, assigned above a risk-reduction cutoff; a predicted harm is read as a confounding artifact and handled like group B, with no CAP (group D); held-out evaluation compares children whose random arm matched the rule (compliers) with those whose did not (defiers) (pp. 2-3, 8).
assumptions: All 607 RIVUR children (302 CAP, 305 placebo; 19 US centers; 2 months-6 years; grade I-IV VUR; 2-year follow-up) (pp. 2-3); predictors limited to information before CAP assignment (p. 2); optimal tree imputation, with creatinine (a split variable) missing in 110 and 115 children per arm (pp. 2, 4, 6); 20% test, 4:1 train/validation per arm, fivefold CV, Julia 0.6.0 and SAS 9.4 (pp. 2-3); admitted: female predominance, low rUTI rate, congenital anomalies excluded, small cohort, BBD not assessable, VUR-grade variability (p. 8).
proof_devices: n/a as a formulation; per-arm two-model risk difference read as treatment benefit (p. 2)
complier/defier contrast on held-out randomized data with a Neyman repeated-sampling test of compliers' ATE <= defiers' ATE (p. 3)
decision table A-D mapping arm risks to decisions, harmful predictions reassigned to no treatment (p. 8)

my reading: with near-equal arms (302 vs 305) compliers and defiers share the covariate mix in expectation, so their gap compares the rule with its opposite and their mean is random assignment (pp. 3, 7)
experiments: AUC 0.82 (0.74-0.87) (p. 3); abstract-only claim that a 10% cutoff treats 40% for minimal population rUTI, with Fig. 4's curve against random described qualitatively (pp. 1, 5, 7); held-out 121: 51 compliers vs 70 defiers, rUTI 7.5% vs 19.4%, p = 0.037 or 0.04 (pp. 1, 7), rates not whole-patient fractions of 51 and 70 (my reading); treat-all and clinicians' selection not scored on held-out data.
positioning: Extends RIVUR (Hoberman et al. 2014) and a meta-analysis by the lead author toward personalized prophylaxis; the methods cited are the group's OCT and optimal tree imputation; personalized-medicine framing (pp. 1-2, 9).
writing: Clinical IMRaD with two patient vignettes that walk the trees (pp. 3-4), a specific limitations paragraph and an 'imperfect' admission (p. 8), followed by two invited editorial comments (pp. 9-10).
limits_future: Generalizability beyond RIVUR's range, small cohort, BBD, VUR grading, overfitting handled only by a held-out set; future: more data and ureteral diameter (p. 8); editorialists (their voice): an arbitrary cutoff behind the AUC, a cumbersome algorithm, not yet clinically applicable (pp. 9-10).

method_links.note: Decisions are scored on held-out randomized data and a population trade-off is drawn, but the owner's current rules (treat all after RIVUR, or clinicians' experience-based selection) are not the scored baseline; the comparison is compliers vs defiers.
One knob (the risk-reduction cutoff) traces the share treated against population rUTI next to random assignment and is left to families and physicians; no bound, the curve shown only as a figure.
The group's tools (OCT, optimal imputation) enter a clinical team's trial reanalysis in a clinical journal, Bertsimas as co-senior author.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: concordance split on held-out randomized data
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Held-out trial patients are split by whether their random arm matched the model's recommendation; compliers vs defiers rUTI 7.5% vs 19.4%, tested on ATEs; with equal arms this compares the rule with its opposite.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: analytics partner inside a clinical team's study
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Boston Children's urologists lead (Wang first and lead author); the MIT side supplies OCT and optimal imputation; Bertsimas is listed among three senior co-last authors in a group byline.

transferable: To score a treatment rule on trial data, split held-out patients by whether their random arm agreed with the rule; with equal arms the outcome gap estimates the rule against its opposite and the mean of the two groups is random assignment (pp. 2-3, 7; the equal-arm argument is my reading).
Fit one model per trial arm and read the treatment benefit as the difference of the two predicted risks; send patients with a predicted harm to no treatment, and say why (pp. 2, 8).
Give the cutoff as a knob with a population curve (share treated vs outcome) next to random allocation, not as one operating point (pp. 4-5, 7).
coauthors: Michael Li (MIT ORC); Carlos Estrada, Caleb Nelson, Hsin-Hsiao Scott Wang (Boston Children's Hospital; Wang first and lead author; Bertsimas, Estrada and Nelson senior co-last authors)

quotes.text: If the model assigned CAP treatment would not bring any benefit compared to baseline, then one expects the ATE of the compliers would be the same as defiers.
It is important to recognize that this prediction model is imperfect, primarily due to the inherent size limitation.

title: Near-optimal nonlinear regression trees
contribution: NNRTs (regression trees with hyperplane splits and MARS-like polynomial leaves, written as one unconstrained nonlinear problem and trained by Adam with ridge-fitted leaves) recover synthetic ground-truth trees and reach a mean out-of-sample R2 of 0.753 on 40 UCI sets against 0.74 for XGBoost and ORT-LH, 0.736 for random forests and 0.71 for MARS, with no optimality certificate (read in the preprint submitted to ORL).
problem_entry: {ML; engine: nonconvex first-order optimization, not MIO} CART is greedy and locally optimal; constant leaves limit regression trees; post-hoc linear leaves give oversize trees, significance-based splits are not optimal, stepwise splits do not extend to hyperplanes; ORT-LH gains 23.4% R2 over CART and MARS fits polynomials greedily; entry: combine MARS and ORT-LH (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Polynomial leaf functions built from |a'x - b| along the path; the identity |a'x - b| 1{a'x < b} = max(b - a'x, 0) makes the tree a sum of hinge products, fitted as one unconstrained problem (squared loss + ridge on a, b, f, 'motivated by robustness considerations'); Adam steps on (a, b) alternate with exact ridge solves for f, started from the best of M random draws (pp. 4-8).
assumptions: Features rescaled to [0, 1] (p. 3); depth D and penalty lambda tuned on validation (pp. 7-8); synthetic polynomial hyperplane trees with D in {2,3,4}, n in {10,000; 100,000}, m in {10, 50, 250}, five trees each, lambda = 0, one start (pp. 7, 9); 40 UCI regression sets with 50/25/25 splits repeated five times (pp. 10-11).
proof_devices: hinge rewriting of indicator-times-distance terms, eq. (3) (p. 6)
block alternation: Adam on split parameters, closed-form ridge regression on leaf coefficients (pp. 6-8)
random multi-start initialization with ridge-fitted leaves (p. 7)
no convergence or optimality analysis; global-optimality claim rests on synthetic ground-truth recovery (pp. 1, 9)
my reading: the objective is only piecewise differentiable although called differentiable (pp. 3, 7)
experiments: 40 UCI sets, depths 1-12, 50 starts, MARS trimmed to depth with tuned penalty, RF, XGBoost (eta 0.1), ORT-LH autotuned; mean R2 0.753 vs 0.74/0.74/0.736/0.71 (Table 4, p. 12); wins 34-6 (MARS), 24-16 (RF), 23-15-2 (XGBoost), 28-12 (ORT-LH) (p. 13); synthetic R2 0.989-0.999 in 20-910 s (pp. 9-10); my reading: text and Table 4 swap the XGBoost/ORT-LH ranks, the claim that depth three outperforms all others at depth twelve is a 0.74 tie with XGBoost and ORT-LH in Table 6, no significance test although refs [21]-[23] are listed (pp. 11-13, 16).
positioning: Places CART, M5, MARS, ORT, ORT-L and ORT-LH in a split x leaf x solution table and fills the empty multivariate-polynomial cell; cites Bertsimas-Copenhaver for the ridge term and claims an edge over all compared methods (pp. 1-5, 14).
writing: A short letter: a three-item contribution list with absolute and percentage R2 gains (p. 3), two synthetic questions answered before the real-data table (p. 7), a two-sentence limitation paragraph (p. 13).
limits_future: Multivariate splits are harder to interpret than univariate ones; training much slower than XGBoost on larger sets (p. 13); no future work stated (p. 14).

method_links.note: One joint model replaces greedy splitting and the greedy incumbent (MARS) is dueled at matched depth with its penalty tuned, but there is no MIO solve, no certificate or gap, a random rather than incumbent warm start, and a global-optimality claim from ground-truth recovery (Tension T1).

Formulation first (the whole tree as one optimization problem), but the class is a nonconvex unconstrained NLP trained by Adam, not LP, conic or MIO; the ridge term follows Heuristic 1 (robustness behind regularization).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Table 1 classifies regression-tree methods by split (uni/multi), leaf (constant/linear/polynomial) and solution (greedy/optimal); NNRT occupies the multivariate-polynomial-'near-optimal' cell.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: first-order surrogate for an MIO-born model class
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The hyperplane tree class of ORT-LH (born as an MIO) is rewritten with hinge products and trained by Adam and ridge regression; compare s20 S331 and S477.

transferable: Rewrite indicator-times-distance terms as hinges, |a'x - b| 1{a'x < b} = max(b - a'x, 0), so a tree's prediction becomes one piecewise-smooth function of its split parameters (p. 6).
Alternate first-order steps on the hard block with an exact closed-form solve on the easy block (ridge for leaf coefficients given the splits) (pp. 6-8).

Before real data, show recovery of synthetic ground truths across (depth, n, m), plus a second test with a linear truth fitted by the polynomial model to show the regularizer suppresses unneeded complexity (pp. 9-10).
Tabulate accuracy against maximum depth for every method, so readers see how shallow the new model can be (Table 6, pp. 12-13).

quotes.text: These experimental results suggest that NNRTs recovered the ground truth and converged to an optimal solution.
Comparing to CART or MARS which use univariate splits, NNRTs use multivariate splits which are harder to interpret.

title: Prediction of neutropenic events in chemotherapy patients: A machine learning approach
contribution: On 17,513 chemotherapy encounters at Hartford HealthCare, a 20-feature sparse additive model (optimal feature selection) predicts severe or febrile neutropenia within 28 days with test AUC 0.865 and the best average precision; it is chosen over a slightly higher-AUC random forest for interpretability, and a cost-ratio analysis puts the G-CSF alert threshold at 8-16% instead of the guideline's 20%.
problem_entry: {ML + AP (oncology); DA in the threshold analysis} SN-FN endangers chemotherapy patients and ASCO recommends G-CSF above 20% risk; existing models are logistic or uninterpretable; gaps: risk at any cycle, broad cancers and drugs, discrete EMR fields only so the model runs off the record (p. 1).
key_idea: An end-to-end pipeline: curated discrete EMR features, MedImpute, six classifiers compared on performance and interpretability, OFS with 20 features as the final score, and a threshold minimizing C_FP x FP + C_FN x FN that depends only on the cost ratio (pp. 1-4).
assumptions: Seven HHC hospitals, May 2016-Oct 2019, leukemia excluded, each cycle an observation (pp. 1-2); outcome SN (ANC < 500) or FN (ANC < 1,000 with fever > 101F) within 28 days; 107 features, those missing in > 40% dropped; 80/20 split by patient, imputed separately, 5-fold CV (p. 2); 2,806 patients, 449 events (2.6%) (p. 4); admitted: retrospective, no causation, structured data only (p. 6).
proof_devices: n/a as a formulation; cost-ratio threshold tau* minimizing C_FP x FP(tau) + C_FN x FN(tau) (pp. 3-4)
split by patient with separate imputation of train and test (p. 2)
average precision reported against a no-skill precision of 0.026 (pp. 3-4)
my reading: the cost-minimizing threshold is computed on the test set, so the reported operating point is chosen in-sample (p. 4)
experiments: Test AUC 0.789-0.869 and AP 0.080-0.148 (Table 3, p. 4): OFS20 0.865/0.148, RF 0.869, LR 0.858, XGB 0.819, OCT 0.805, CART 0.789; NSCLC example with ratio 8.5 gives tau 0.16, specificity 95.7%, sensitivity 42.9%; threshold 16% for ratios 5-10 and 8% for 15-30 (p. 4) vs guideline 20% (p. 6); Lyman et al. (AUC 0.81) compared by citation only (p. 5).
positioning: Sets itself against logistic neutropenia models (Lyman et al., Hosmer et al.) and uninterpretable ML (Cho et al., Holborow et al.), claiming a better AUC than Lyman's 0.81 and calling Cho's 0.908 a narrower question (pp. 1, 5).
writing: Clinical IMRaD with a Context box (Key Objective, Knowledge Generated, Relevance) (p. 2); final-model choice argued on interpretability (p. 4); causation hedged (p. 6).
limits_future: Retrospective, no causation (p. 6); benefits of true positives and negatives and nonfinancial costs (alarm fatigue, quality of life) not modelled (pp. 6-7); prospective validation within HHC and at external sites hoped for (p. 7); data not shareable (IRB) (p. 7).

method_links.note: The owner (Hartford HealthCare) and its decision (G-CSF, EMR alerts) are named and the 20% guideline is the reference, but the guideline rule is not scored on the same cost metric and the main evaluation is AUC and AP, not decisions.
The cost ratio is one knob and the threshold-vs-ratio curve (Fig. 2) is handed to each institution for 'tailoring algorithms to individual hospital needs'; no bound.

The group's own optimal tree loses (OCT 0.805 vs LR 0.858) and the paper says so, reading it as weak nonlinear interactions (step 6, Heuristic 4); OFS20 chosen over a slightly higher-AUC random forest for interpretability (Taste mark 5).
Partner-funded student project (Wiberg) built on the group's tools (OFS, MedImpute), published in a clinical journal.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: cost-ratio threshold curve for a risk score
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The alert threshold minimizes C_FP x FP + C_FN x FN, depends only on C_FN/C_FP, and is published as a curve (16% for ratios 5-10, 8% for 15-30) set against the 20% guideline.

transferable: Turn a risk score into a decision by minimizing C_FP x FP(tau) + C_FN x FN(tau); only the ratio matters, so publish tau* as a function of C_FN/C_FP and mark the guideline threshold on it (pp. 3-4, 6); choose tau on validation data, not the test set (my reading).
When a patient contributes many encounters, split train and test by patient and impute the two sets separately (p. 2).
Restrict inputs to discrete EMR fields so other sites can run the model directly off their records, and say what that leaves out (pp. 2, 6-7).
With 2.6% positives, report average precision next to AUC with the no-skill precision (0.026) as reference (pp. 3-4).
coauthors: Holly Wiberg (MIT ORC); Peter Yu, Pat Montanaro, Jeff Mather, Suzi Birz, Michelle Schneider (Hartford HealthCare); Bertsimas corresponding author

quotes.text: Overall, the strength of the linear models suggests that nonlinear feature interactions are not highly significant in this prediction problem.
The optimal threshold is determined purely by the cost ratio.

title: Optimizing influenza vaccine composition: A machine learning approach
contribution: A three-layer pipeline (drift-constrained tensor completion of global circulation rates, optimal regression trees linking antigenic distance to morbidity and mortality, and a robust strain choice over the latent factors reformulated as an SOCP via a minimax swap) is claimed, in a retrospective 2009-2018 comparison, to lower predicted morbidity by 8-14% and mortality by 6-11% relative to WHO, FDA and EMA compositions (read in the MIT author manuscript).
problem_entry: {DA + RO + ML; AP (public health)} WHO, FDA and EMA reformulate the flu vaccine yearly, 6-8 months ahead, and emerging strains are hard to predict; earlier OR models (stochastic DP, optimal stopping, bilevel) model the committee's keep-or-switch choice, do not identify emerging strains from data, and neither prescribe by region nor quantify morbidity and mortality (pp. 3, 5-6).
key_idea: Low-rank completion of the country x virus x season tensor with ||S^t - S^(t-1)||_F <= lambda (SVD of unfoldings for U, V; one SOCP for the cores); ORTs from circulation-weighted antigenic distances to morbidity and mortality; a robust strain choice minimizing the worst-case weighted distance over Y = U S V' with ||S - S_hat||_F^2 <= lambda, swapped to max-min and solved as an SOCP (pp. 3-4, 9-14).
assumptions: GISRS tensor 1987-2018 (T = 32, m = 1,206 viruses, n about 132 countries, about 88% missing) (pp. 3, 9); HI distances d_uv = log(max_u h_uv / h_uv) for 1,377 viruses x 82 vaccine strains (p. 9); outcome estimates from CDC, ECDC, GISRS, Iuliano et al. (p. 9); r and lambda by cross-validation, ORT parameters on a holdout set (p. 11); latent weights assumed not to change drastically across seasons (p. 4); nominal forecast = last season's core S^(T-1) (p. 13).
proof_devices: alternating tensor completion: SVD of mode-1 and mode-2 unfoldings for U and V, an SOCP in T r^2 variables for the cores (pp. 10-11)
uncertainty set on the latent core of the factorization (p. 14)
minimax swap stated as Lemma 3.1 (von Neumann 1928) and reformulation to SOCP (8) (pp. 13-14)

my reading: the swap needs a convex strategy set; over vertices z in {0,1}^q max-min can be strictly below min-max (two strains with costs y and 1 - y give 1/2 vs 1), so SOCP (8) is the randomized-strain value, a lower bound, and the returned strain is a best response to the worst case (pp. 13-14)
experiments: Retrospective 2009/10-2018/19, predicted morbidity and mortality under robust vs WHO, CDC/FDA (USA and four states) and EMA compositions by ORTs on 20-year moving windows (pp. 15-17; Tables 1-7, pp. 19-22); claimed 11-14%/8-11% (WHO), 8-10%/6-9% (FDA), 10-12%/9-11% (EMA) (p. 2); strain closer in 3-6 of 'ten' seasons (pp. 16-17); my reading: outcome-model error on historical choices exceeds the effect (FDA 2011-12: 9.3 observed vs 24.7 predicted million severe illnesses, Table 6, p. 22), the nominal model is never scored, Tables 8 and 12 carry identical distance columns, Table 1 (2017-18) and Table 5 (2018-19) share their illness entries, Table 7 captioned USA but discussed as Europe (pp. 16, 19-26); no run times.
positioning: Reviews genomic and phylogenetic prediction (Neher et al., Luksza-Lassig) and OR strain-selection models (Wu-Wein-Perelson, Kornish-Keeney, Cho, Ozaltin et al.); claims to be the first to use tensor completion, ORTs and robust optimization for vaccine composition (pp. 4-6).
writing: 'holistic framework' and 'state-of-the-art methods' in abstract and conclusion; a contribution list with percentage gains; the hedge 'could potentially lower' repeated (pp. 2, 6-7, 15-17); no limitations section.
limits_future: No limitations or future work are stated (Conclusions, p. 17); the only hedge is 'could potentially' (pp. 2, 15-17).

method_links.note: The owners' actual decisions (WHO, FDA, EMA compositions) are the baselines and decisions are scored, but outcomes are predicted by trees whose input is the optimized quantity, with no observed counterfactual or field test.

The robust choice is kept in a solvable class (SOCP), but the device is not checked on a small example; on two strains the swap fails (my reading), which is the exactness check Method 1's correction asks for.

One knob lambda, described as the season-to-season drift of the latent core, bounds both the completion and the uncertainty set and is chosen by cross-validation (as the correction asks), but no curve over lambda is shown.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Counterfactual replay against the historical decision-maker
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Each season 2009/10-2018/19 is replayed with the robust composition and with the WHO, FDA or EMA composition, both scored by the same ORT outcome model on observed circulation.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: uncertainty set on the predictor's latent factors, sized by its drift budget
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The robust set is a Frobenius ball on the low-rank core S of the forecasting factorization, the same season-to-season drift restriction that constrains the tensor completion, so the counterpart stays a small SOCP.

transferable: Put the uncertainty set on the forecasting model's low-dimensional latent core (Y = U S V', ||S - S_hat||_F bounded) rather than on the high-dimensional forecast, so the robust counterpart stays a small SOCP (pp. 13-14).
For a time-indexed low-rank model, bound the drift of the core by ||S^t - S^(t-1)||_F <= lambda; SVDs of the unfoldings give the shared factors and one SOCP gives the cores (pp. 9-11).
Before a minimax swap over a discrete choice, relax it to the simplex and check on a two-option example whether min-max equals max-min (my reading of pp. 13-14).
When counterfactual outcomes are predicted, report the outcome model's error on the incumbent's actual decisions next to the claimed gain (my reading of Table 6, p. 22).
coauthors: Hari Bandi (MIT ORC); Bertsimas corresponding author

quotes.text: Observe that Problem (5) is very sensitive to the predicted rates of circulation of viruses.
for a given geographical location represented by i, the objective function of Problem (6) is bilinear in z and Yi

title: Prescriptive machine learning for public policy: The case of immigration enforcement
contribution: An optimal classification tree predicting Level 1 re-arrest from 904,896 FOIA detainer records is evaluated against ICE's decisions through a natural experiment (prison security classification plus ICE's tendency to detain near its offices); it is estimated to cut Level 1 crime by 24-28% at fixed detention capacity, and by more than ICE or the DHS priority rule when capacity expands.
problem_entry: {DA + ML; AP (public policy)} $380 billion of enforcement spending with little evidence of crime reduction; ICE targets low-priority immigrants while ignoring high-priority ones; a practical, not causal, question: can crime-risk predictions design a crime-preventing policy, with the evaluation under unobserved confounding as the stated primary innovation (pp. 2-3, 6).
key_idea: OCT trained on non-detained recipients ranks risk; the top recipients are deported at ICE's capacity; evaluation via prison classification (comparable inmates within type x security bins) plus ICE's distance-driven detainment (AUC 0.701): a one-sided test expanding detainment in far prisons, and a fixed-resource test swapping deportations across tree leaves with a Wald-ratio (LATE) estimate of the crime added by releases (pp. 10-19).
assumptions: Universe of detainers Oct 2008-Nov 2015 via FOIA; 17.1% duplicates removed, 9.6% missing sentences imputed by ML, 4.7% still in prison dropped; 904,896 detainers, 60/40 split (pp. 7-8); features include citizenship, country of birth and gender (p. 11); federal and CA/TX state prisons in nine bins (p. 14); deportees assumed to commit no further US crime (pp. 15, 19); bins similar 'as an empirical matter' though prisons and offices are not randomly placed (fn 7, pp. 13-14).
proof_devices: identity splitting the crime change at fixed capacity into an observed reduction and an unobserved increase (p. 12)
natural experiment: security-classification bins x distance to the ICE field office as plausibly exogenous variation, with a within-bin balance check (pp. 13-14)
one-sided test needing no counterfactual model: add deportations only among non-deported inmates of far prisons up to nearer prisons' rates (pp. 15-17)
Wald-ratio estimator delta(l, b), a LATE under Angrist-Imbens-Rubin assumptions; the test is necessary, sufficient only under unconfoundedness (p. 19, fn 12-13)
asymptotic confidence intervals adapted from Imbens-Rubin (p. 20)
experiments: AUC 0.786 (p. 11); detainment gaps 9.91/14.78/25.48 points by distance quartile (p. 14); one-sided: crime reduction 16.7/26.1/41.2% (algorithm) vs 9.5/15.1/23.9% (ICE) vs 7.9/12.6/20.8% (DHS rule), all above random (Table 2, pp. 16-18); fixed resources: 0.1076 -> 0.0776 federal (-27.82%), 0.1537 -> 0.1173 state (-23.63%) (p. 20); headline 26% (pp. 1, 3, 21) vs 25% (p. 22).
positioning: Departs from causal immigration-crime work (Pinotti's RD, Miles-Cox's DiD) toward prediction-to-policy, and from recidivism forecasting that rarely meets human decisions; closest are bail studies (Jung et al. under unconfoundedness; Kleinberg et al. via random judge assignment) and a predictive-policing RCT (Mohler et al.) (pp. 6-7).
writing: The evaluation is announced as the primary innovation (p. 3); the headline percentage leads the abstract; the key assumptions sit in footnotes (fn 7, 12-15); the discussion argues algorithms need not be worse than the humans they augment (p. 22).
limits_future: The 26% is specific to federal and state prisons and to distance-based variation (p. 21); other goals of enforcement are not modelled (p. 21); it assumes ICE could follow the ranking perfectly (fn 14, p. 21); ethical and legal review and a subgroup check must precede deployment (p. 22).

method_links.note: The owner's actual decisions (ICE) and its written rule (DHS priorities) are scored as separate baselines beside random choice, decisions are compared at matched capacity, and what the evaluation cannot show is stated; no field test (step 6 partial); OCT chosen for interpretability given the stakes (Taste mark 5).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Counterfactual replay against the historical decision-maker
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Variant: ICE's historical detainment is replayed at equal capacity and location, with confounding handled by a natural experiment instead of matching.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: natural-experiment scoring of a prescriptive policy
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Prison security classification makes inmates comparable within bins, and distance to the ICE office shifts detainment (AUC 0.701); this variation scores the algorithm against ICE by one-sided and Wald-ratio tests.

transferable: Evaluate a recommender against human decisions with a natural experiment: a variable that shifts the human decision but not the population (here distance to the deciding office within security-level bins); check balance within bins and use it to estimate outcomes of those the policy would release (pp. 13-19).

Run a one-sided test that needs no counterfactual model: only add treatments to untreated units, whose outcome under treatment is known, up to the treatment rate observed in comparable units (pp. 15-17).
Hold capacity and the location of decisions fixed when comparing a policy with the incumbent (pp. 12, 18).
Score the incumbent's written rule (DHS guidelines) and its actual behaviour (ICE) as separate baselines, plus random (pp. 16-17).

quotes.text: While developing the machine learning algorithm is a major task on its own, the paper’s primary innovation is how we evaluate whether the algorithm’s recommendations improve upon ICE’s decisions.
the 26% (average) reduction in crime can be interpreted as what would have happened if ICE could logistically follow our algorithm’s prioritization perfectly.

title: Hurricane forecasting: A novel multimodal machine learning framework
contribution: Hurricast concatenates frozen deep-learning embeddings of ERA5 reanalysis maps with storm statistics and predicts 24-hour track and intensity with XGBoost; on 2016-2019 North Atlantic and Eastern Pacific cases it is competitive in intensity but well behind dynamical models in North Atlantic track, while adding it to a simple operational consensus beats NHC's official forecast by 2-14% in MAE, ignoring operational lag (read in arXiv v4).
problem_entry: {ML; AP (weather); no optimization model or decision} Track and intensity forecasts drive life-saving measures; operational forecasts are dynamical, statistical, statistical-dynamical, ensemble or consensus; ML had used RNNs on historical tracks and CNNs on reanalysis or satellite data; entry: one multimodal ML framework judged against the operational models (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Three steps: embed reanalysis-map sequences with a supervised CNN encoder plus GRU or Transformer decoder, frozen and read at its penultimate layer (128 of 45,000 features), or with an unsupervised Tucker decomposition; concatenate with storm statistics; one XGBoost per task; ElasticNet stacking and an operational consensus as variants (pp. 4-6).
assumptions: IBTrACS since 1980, storms reaching 34 kt with > 60 h of data: 2,599 storms, 133,999 cases (pp. 2-3); ERA5 25 x 25 degree maps of z, u, v at three levels over eight steps (pp. 3, 5); ATCF operational forecasts (pp. 3-4); train 1980-2011, validation 2012-2015, test 2016-2019, test on NA and EP only (p. 7); admitted: reanalysis not real-time and misrepresents storm size (p. 3); operational lag ignored (pp. 8, 12).
proof_devices: n/a (no formulation or proof); a supervised encoder frozen as a feature extractor, 'inspired by transfer learning and distillation' (p. 5)
Tucker decomposition of the 8 x 9 x 25 x 25 map tensor as an unsupervised alternative, core rank tuned on validation (pp. 5-6, 12)
stacking on held-out years: base models trained to 2011, ElasticNet fitted on their 2012-2015 forecasts, tested on 2016-2019 (p. 12)
experiments: Same cases for all models (837/899 track, 877/899 intensity); track skill 40% (EP) and 46% (NA) vs HWRF 45/63% and GFSO 46/65% (Table 5, p. 8); intensity MAE 12% better than Decay-SHIPS and 3% than HWRF in EP, 2% and 7% worse in NA (p. 7); consensus with HUML beats OFCL by 8%/2% (intensity) and 7%/14% (track) (p. 8); one V100 GPU, forecasts in seconds, code public (p. 7); my reading: 'comparable' covers a 109 km NA track MAE against 71-75 km (p. 8).
positioning: Places itself among dynamical, statistical and consensus operational models and earlier RNN/CNN work, borrowing the CNN encoder from Giffard-Roisin et al.; claims the first Transformer-decoder in tropical cyclone forecasting (pp. 1-2, 9, 11).
writing: A lay significance statement (p. 1), three numbered contributions (p. 2), results as three claims (i)-(iii) (pp. 7-8), and a limitations-and-extensions section (pp. 8-9).
limits_future: Reanalysis maps block real-time use; train on real-time observations or reforecasts; add sea-surface temperature, humidity, satellite and radar data; extend beyond 24 h (NHC forecasts 5 days) (pp. 8-9).

method_links.note: The owner's own forecasts (OFCL, operational models) are the baselines on identical cases, scored on the field's metrics (MAE, skill vs CLP5 and Decay-SHIPS) as the correction asks, but no decision is made and the operational lag favouring the ML model is acknowledged rather than removed.
Student-led line (Boussioux, Zeng) with industry funding (OCP Group), released code and open data, published in the field's journal.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: frozen modular extractors producing one patient vector
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Here a storm vector: frozen encoder-decoder embeddings of reanalysis maps concatenated with tabular storm features for one boosted learner, extractors swappable per data source; compare c23 S023, c2-08 S439.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: second stage fitted on held-out first-stage outputs
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The ElasticNet ensemble is trained on base-model forecasts for 2012-2015, years the base models never saw, and tested on 2016-2019.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: score the new model as a member of the incumbent's consensus
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Besides the standalone duel, the best HUML model is added to a simple average of operational forecasts, which then beats NHC's official forecast in both tasks and basins.

transferable: Score a new forecaster both on its own and as an added member of the incumbent's consensus; a gain inside the consensus shows complementarity even when it is weaker alone (pp. 7-8).
Freeze a supervised encoder and feed its penultimate layer to a gradient-boosted model; keep one swappable extractor per modality (pp. 5, 9).
Fit the stacking model on forecasts for years the base models never saw, then test on later years (p. 12).
Train on every region with data but report only where the incumbent's forecasts exist, on identical cases (p. 7).
coauthors: Leonard Boussioux and Cynthia Zeng (MIT ORC, equal contribution), Theo Guenais (Harvard SEAS); Bertsimas corresponding author

quotes.text: As a remark, we do not consider the computational time lag of operational model forecasts in our experiments.
Thus, although our models can compute forecasts in seconds, the dependence on reanalysis maps is a bottleneck in real-time forecasting.

title: Optimal survival trees
contribution: Optimal Survival Trees carry the Optimal Trees coordinate-descent local search to censored data with a LeBlanc-Crowley likelihood node error; in simulations with known true trees and on 44 UCI sets with synthetic censoring they recover structure and survival curves better than rpart and ctree, with no significant gain on the Cox ratio or Harrell's C (read in arXiv v1).
problem_entry: {ML (IO named, local search used); AP (health)} Cox regression misses nonlinearities and interactions; survival trees are grown greedily; forests are black boxes; the two user-friendly public implementations are rpart and ctree; problem: Optimal-Trees survival trees plus metrics able to rank survival trees (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Coordinate descent over splits (delete, re-optimize, add) from random starting trees until no move improves error + alpha x complexity; a node-separable error (LeBlanc-Crowley likelihood, Nelson-Aalen baseline, closed-form leaf coefficient, deviance against the saturated model); new simulation metrics: node homogeneity, class recovery and the Kaplan-Meier area ratio (pp. 3-6, 9-11).
assumptions: Proportional-hazards node model with a Nelson-Aalen baseline (p. 5); simulations: 1,000 sets of 20,000 observations, six covariates, random true trees of depth 3-4 with exponential, Weibull, lognormal or gamma leaves, censoring kappa(1 - u^2) at 0-80%, n from 100 to 10,000 (pp. 12, 29); 44 UCI regression sets with synthetic censoring, selection 'independent of the analysis of model accuracy' (p. 19); Framingham CHD patients (pp. 20-21).
proof_devices: node-separable error so local moves re-score only the changed subtree (p. 5)
closed-form leaf hazard coefficient and deviance against the saturated model (eqs. 5-8, pp. 5-6)
paired structure metrics with opposite biases: node homogeneity (favours large trees) and class recovery (favours small trees) (p. 10)
Kaplan-Meier area ratio against the true survival curves (p. 11)
no MIO solve, optimality analysis or run times; 'globally optimized' (p. 1) vs a locally optimal stopping rule (p. 4)
experiments: rpart and ctree cross-validated with OST's own error (eq. 7) as score, OST tuned internally (p. 12); simulations: OST best on node homogeneity/class recovery (87/91 vs 82/79 and 85/50 at n = 10,000) and KM area ratio (84.41 vs 80.06, 73.57) (pp. 13, 16); UCI: better on average, significant only for Uno's C and the Brier ratios, undominated in 48.7-59.3% vs 27.3-38.4% (p. 20); my reading: OST trails rpart on some metrics at 30% and 80% censoring (p. 41); Framingham Brier scores given without direction (p. 22).
positioning: Reviews survival trees (Gordon-Olshen, LeBlanc-Crowley, Therneau, Hothorn's ctree, Molinaro's IPCW) and survival forests as black boxes, and builds on Optimal Trees (Bertsimas-Dunn 2017, 2019; Dunn 2018) (pp. 2-4).
writing: Four numbered contributions (p. 2); a figure from the OCT work reproduced to motivate (Fig. 1, p. 5); a Framingham example contrasting OST's BMI threshold 25.031 with the greedy 24.117 as evidence of global vs local optimization (p. 22).
limits_future: KM curves poor in small leaves, so a minimum node size of about 50 is advised (p. 15); stability necessary but not sufficient for accuracy (pp. 16-19); the field's metrics disagree in about 70% of instances (p. 9); no future work section (p. 22).

method_links.note: One joint objective replaces greedy splitting, the incumbent's standard implementations (rpart, ctree) are dueled on identical data with cross-validated parameters, and non-winning metrics are printed (step 6); but no MIO is solved, no certificate or gap is given, and a locally optimal tree is called 'globally optimized' (Tension T1, T6).
Programme extension OCT -> OST with students and Dunn (Interpretable AI address); software under an academic license by e-mail.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: audit the field's headline metric before competing on it
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Cox scores and C-statistics are shown to be inflated by tied risks and extra nodes, and the standard metrics leave no undominated model in about 70% of comparisons, which motivates simulation metrics.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: simulate, then recover, with known truth
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Random ground-truth trees with known leaf survival distributions; recovery scored by node homogeneity, class recovery and the KM area ratio against the true curves.
Node homogeneity is perfect for a saturated tree and class recovery for a null tree, so the two are reported side by side (Table 1).

transferable: When the field's metrics disagree, simulate from a known ground-truth model and score structure recovery and curve recovery directly (pp. 9-12).
Pair two structure metrics biased in opposite directions (node homogeneity favours large trees, class recovery small ones) and always report them together (p. 10).
Choose an error that is evaluable node by node so that a local search re-scores only the changed subtree (p. 5).
Separate stability from accuracy: compare trees trained on disjoint samples and add covariate noise to the training data only (pp. 16-19).
State the exclusion criteria for benchmark data sets and that selection was independent of results (fn 4, p. 19).
coauthors: Jack Dunn (Interpretable AI address), Emma Gibson, Agni Orfanoudaki (MIT ORC)

title: Two-stage sample robust optimization
contribution: Giving each data point's ball-shaped uncertainty set its own linear decision rule turns two-stage sample robust optimization (type-infinity Wasserstein DRO) into an LP or SOCP of size O(N) that upper-bounds the robust problem and, as the balls shrink, converges almost surely to the stochastic optimum, also without relatively complete recourse; in experiments it stays feasible where SAA does not and matches the event-wise DRO approximation while running far faster than the SDP one (read in arXiv v4).
problem_entry: {RO + DA; SD (two-stage stochastic LP); LO as engine} SAA is a linear-size LP and asymptotically optimal but optimistically biased with few data and, without relatively complete recourse, may need impractically many points to be feasible; Wasserstein DRO helps out of sample but two-stage (D)RO is NP-hard; own earlier limit: the multistage SRO paper did not analyze the tightness of its decision-rule approximations (pp. 2-4).
key_idea: Average over data points the worst-case second-stage cost on a ball of radius eps_N around each point intersected with a support superset (SAA at eps_N = 0); approximate it by N overlapping linear decision rules, one per ball, which is a valid upper bound because the second stage need not be non-anticipative, reformulated by duality as an O(N) LP or SOCP, and asymptotically optimal as eps_N -> 0 (pp. 6-12).
assumptions: Two-stage stochastic LP with right-hand-side uncertainty h(xi) = h0 + H xi; i.i.d. data and a known polyhedral superset of the support (p. 6); [A1] linear rules and eps_N -> 0, [A2]-[A3] SAA-style conditions, not verifiable but standard (p. 12); [A4] LDR feasibility in every small ball: sufficient check by one RO problem (Prop. 2, p. 13), equivalent to [A5] and [A6] (Lemma 1, pp. 14-15), no counterexample found, open (pp. 12-13, 16).
proof_devices: Theorem 1: overlapping local policies give an upper bound by picking the best rule per realization (pp. 10-11)
Proposition 1: Lagrangian duality turns MP with linear rules into an LP (l1, l-infinity) or SOCP (l2) with O(N) size (p. 11)

sandwich proof of Theorem 2: liminf via SAA consistency (King-Wets, Robinson), limsup via a step toward x* (Lemma 2) and a cost bound for local rules (Lemma 3) using finitely many recourse matrices ([A6]); decisions via Robinson's epiconvergence (pp. 16-21)
minimal faces of the support and radii of polyhedra with Hoffman's lemma for [A4]-[A6] (pp. 14-15, 34-38)
Appendix D: type-infinity Wasserstein concentration (Trillos-Slepcev) giving a rate for eps_N and a finite-sample guarantee, plus Example 3 where SRO is feasible and SAA is not (pp. 52-55)
experiments: M = 100 training sets per N from 16 to 512, test set of 10^4 points, v* by SAA on 10^5 (pp. 22-23); inventory network (n = 10, no complete recourse, eps_N = 10 or 20 N^(-1/10)): MP far more often feasible than SAA, gap near zero at N = 512 while SP's grows, DRO baselines forced to x = (K, ..., K), 0.4-1.5 s per data point (pp. 24-26); medical scheduling (n = 8): MP matches Wass SW and SAA, overestimates cost by 5-10% while SAA underestimates in 50-80% of sets, 9.96 s vs 323 s for Wass SDP at N = 512 (p. 28); no solver or machine named; Fig. 3 gaps averaged only over sets feasible on the whole test set (p. 26).
positioning: Builds on SAA theory (Shapiro, King-Wets, Robinson), DRO (Delage-Ye, Wiesemann et al.), two-stage Wasserstein approximations (Hanasusanto-Kuhn, Chen et al.) and the group's multistage SRO; acknowledges Xie 2020 as follow-up and Chen et al. as independent but without asymptotic analysis (pp. 2-5).
writing: Contribution bullets point to Theorem 1, Proposition 1 and Theorem 2 (p. 3); an aim statement scopes the paper away from finite-sample guarantees (p. 4); candid open questions ('despite our efforts') (pp. 12-13, 16); the method is repeatedly called 'simple' (pp. 1, 28).
limits_future: Whether [A4] is equivalent to feasibility is open (p. 16); the constants in the eps_N rate depend on the unknown distribution (p. 53); cross-validation of the radius is suggested but not run (p. 24); extension to other DRO settings likely needs sets that shrink with N (pp. 29-30).

method_links.note: An NP-hard robust problem (fn 1) is approximated inside the LP/SOCP class at size O(N) through Lagrangian duality, and the boundary is printed (NP-hardness, the open [A4] question).
One knob, eps_N, with a rate from a concentration theorem but a hand-set constant (10, 20, 1); cross-validation suggested but not run; no curve over eps_N.

Decisions are scored out of sample (expected cost, feasibility, prediction error) against SAA, the field's standard rule, and three DRO rivals with run times, but on synthetic instances with no owner.
Sturt's sample-robust-optimization student line in the DA programme; two-stage companion of the multistage paper (S113, card c2-06).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: asymptotic optimality as the warrant for a simple heuristic
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The multi-policy approximation, called simple, is justified by Theorem 2's almost-sure convergence to the stochastic optimum under SAA-like conditions.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: subsume the incumbent as a special case
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: SRO with eps_N = 0 is SAA (Remark 1), and the multi-policy approximation reduces to the single-policy one when the rules are forced equal.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: own earlier result's limit as the entry
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The group's multistage SRO paper approximated SRO by linear or piecewise-linear rules but 'does not analyze the tightness of these approximations'.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: one local policy per sample, overlap allowed
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Each data point's uncertainty set gets its own linear decision rule; overlapping, even contradictory, rules still bound the two-stage robust problem because nothing remains to anticipate after the second-stage uncertainty is revealed (Theorem 1).

transferable: In a two-stage robust problem, give each data point's uncertainty set its own recourse rule; overlapping rules still give a valid upper bound because the second stage has nothing left to anticipate (Theorem 1, pp. 10-11).
Prove asymptotic optimality of a data-driven approximation by a sandwich: lower bound from SAA's known consistency, upper bound from a feasible perturbation of the true optimum (pp. 20-21).

For an opaque assumption, give a cheap sufficient check (one RO feasibility problem, Prop. 2), an exact characterization (Lemma 1), and test both on an example where the simple check fails (Example 2) (pp. 13-15).
Report a 'prediction error' (in-sample optimal value vs out-of-sample cost) to show whether a method's value is a reliable upper bound (pp. 23, 25, 28).
coauthors: Shimrit Shtern (Technion), Bradley Sturt (University of Illinois at Chicago)
